newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Telecom firms gear up for 1998 EU liberalisation.
newsitem.headline: Telecom firms gear up for 1998 EU liberalisation.

text.p: The privatisation of Deutsche Telekom takes place amid a frenzy of activity in the European Union telecommunications market as companies scramble to get in shape for a new era of free competition.

The planned merger between British Telecommunications Plc and MCI Communications Corp is the latest in a wave of deals struck in the runup to January 1, 1998 -- the deadline the EU has set for abolishing state telecoms monopolies in most of its 15 countries.
That move follows EU clearance of the Global One trans-Atlantic alliance between France Telecom, Deutsche Telekom and Sprint Corp.

"It's quite clear that Europe will be looking at about four or five big telephone companies, with the others being marginal national or regional players," said Peter Alexiadis, a telecommunications lawyer at Squire, Sanders and Dempsey in Brussels.

The 1998 deadline will force governments, which have been gradually liberalising their telecoms markets since the late 1980s under pressure from the European Commission, to open up their lucrative voice phone sectors.

While companies plot their strategy, the EU is rushing to wrap up a legislative package to regulate the new environment, covering issues such as telecoms licenses and ensuring access to affordable basic phone services.

Analysts said the EU was generally keeping to its liberalisation timetable, at least on paper, but warned that some important regulatory questions had still not been fully addressed -- such as how to ensure that competitors have fair access to each other's networks.

"Just having the market open for competition still doesn't guarantee that you'll have a normal competitive functioning market from the first of January 1998, or ever," said Keith Mallinson, managing director of telecoms consultancy Yankee Group Europe.

He said new market players in some countries will face a tremendous challenge competing with the dominant presence and infrastructure of the traditional monopolies -- along the lines of trying to compete with Coca-Cola or Pepsi-Cola.
"You and I can start a cola company tomorrow, but we'd still have the legacy of their overwhelming presence," he said.
COMMISSION PUSHES TO MEET DEADLINE
But the move in Europe towards global alliances has given the Commission, a powerful weapon for prodding governments to do as much as they can to move the process along.
It agreed to clear the Global One venture, for example, only after Bonn and Paris pledged to open up their markets for telecoms infrastructure.
Facing additional pressure from the Commission over Deutsche Telekom, Bonn issued licenses in October to Telekom rivals Vebacom GmbH, NetCologne and Colt Telecom.
The Commission most recently turned to Spain, which has the right under EU law to request a five-year delay to the market-opening timetable.
The EU executive told Madrid last month that it wanted it to renounce the "derogation", saying it was critical to the World Trade Organisation telecoms liberalisation talks.

It also hinted that it would otherwise block participation by Spanish phone company Telefonica de Espana SA, Europe's fifth largest operator, in the Unisource joint venture with three other European phone companies. That venture has entered a global alliance with AT&T Corp.

The Commission announced on Monday that Spain had now agreed to have legislation in place for full liberalisation by the end of July 1998 and to issue licenses for voice telephone operators by the end of November 1998.

The Commission is expected to decide later this year whether to allow Greece, Ireland, Portugal and Luxembourg to delay liberalisation -- a possibility granted by EU governments during tough negotiations on the 1998 deadline.

Arguing that a competitive telecoms market is essential for industrial competitiveness, the Commission has regularly used special powers under Article 90 of the EC Treaty to pry open telecoms sectors.

It ordered governments to introduce full competition in their mobile phone markets last January. It ordered them last year to allow cable TV networks by January 1, 1996 to carry telecoms services such as data transmission that had already been opened to competition.
LEGISLATION IN PLACE BUT OBSTACLES REMAIN
The Commission has said that the necessary national legislation was largely in place and it is now turning its attention to ensuring that the letter and spirit of the deadlines are followed.

"The real work is starting now," EU Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert told a recent conference. "The environment is in place, the legislation is there. But to make it happen in the real world is another thing."

Van Miert is expected to issue a notice soon on an issue that is critical for new market players: how it will handle complaints about unfair terms for "interconnection" agreements allowing competitors access to the dominant operator's network.
Alexiadis said effective competition could be delayed while EU states get new licensing regimes into place: "January 1, 1998 in most cases will be more realistically sometime in 1999."

EU telecommunications ministers provisionally agreed a directive on licensing in September, but watered down the Commission proposal to give governments more leeway to require companies to apply for individual licenses rather than falling under a "general authorisation scheme".

British Telecom, which operates in one of Europe's most open telecoms markets, complained in a recent statement that EU legislation gives little guidance to national regulators on some key questions -- for example, how to determine what prices companies can charge for interconnections.

BT is among a number of companies that have called for the creation of a pan-European telecoms regulatory system, fearing that national authorities will continue to favour their traditional operators or interpret EU rules differently.
But the Commission has shied away from making such a proposal, which would be highly controversial with some EU governments.

"The idea of a Euroregulator is going to come up again and again. Once we are beyond January 1, 1998 and have an idea about how things are developing -- then and only then can the debate really take off," Alexiadis said.
